column3: It gives the closest parallel: disbelievers are struck on their faces and backs and made to taste the blazing punishment.
Its procedure for replacing witnesses in a testimony dispute does not clarify the threatened exposure to Fire.
The divine withholding of hostile hands provides a limited inverse of the disbelievers' inability to ward anything off themselves.
It directly states that the disbelievers' schemes avail nothing and that they will not be helped.
As immediate context, it denies human immortality and sets the mortal horizon for the warning addressed to the mockers.
The restraint of opposing hands is a contrary instance of protection, not the Fire's inescapable exposure.
It directly depicts the Fire scorching their faces, specifying the facial exposure in the focus ayah.
The immediately preceding taunt, asking when the promise will come, is answered by the focus ayah's warning.
Its futile reaching hands toward water offers a distant image of an ineffective attempt, without the focus ayah's punishment scene.
It explicitly says that the Fire covers their faces, closely paralleling the focus ayah.
The instruction not to hasten the signs supplies the nearby response to the demand for the promised punishment.
It repeats the Day when no ally can avail another and they receive no help, though it is redundant after 52:46.
The concern for testimony given correctly is unrelated to the Fire and helplessness in the focus ayah.
It frames the Day as one in which compensation, intercession, and help fail, broadening the stated lack of aid.
Its local reminder of death, trial, and return establishes the larger reckoning horizon of this warning sequence.
It again denies all help on the Day, but adds little beyond the earlier, closely parallel statements.
The next ayah explains the threat: it will come suddenly, leave them unable to repel it, and allow no delay.
Leaders who call toward the Fire and receive no help supply a related collective trajectory of punishment.
The local warning and the deafness of those warned identify the rejected admonition behind the coming punishment.
Concealing oneself beneath clothing concerns divine knowledge of secrets, not inability to repel the Fire.
Its question about destruction for others' wrongdoing only distantly concerns punishment and does not explain this scene.
It portrays future regret by disbelievers, a fitting response once the presently denied threat is known.
The nearby depiction of their mockery and disbelief supplies the attitude to which the focus warning responds.
The disobedient disbelievers' wish to be levelled with the earth conveys the remorse of exposed judgment.
Its immediate sequel says that what the mockers ridiculed will encompass them, carrying the warning forward.
It joins darkened faces, lack of protection from God, and abiding in the Fire, though not the front-and-back image.
Their boast that they are a united victorious group sharply contrasts with the focus ayah's declaration that none will help them.
The primordial testimony and later excuse of heedlessness do not materially clarify the threatened Fire.
The local question of who can guard them from the Merciful directly anticipates their lack of protection.
The white faces of those in mercy form only a general contrary outcome to the condemned faces in the focus ayah.
It directly denies that their alleged gods can protect even themselves or give aid, explaining the claimed absence of help.
The Hour's sudden arrival and the sinners' burdens upon their backs parallel the surprise and back-oriented exposure.
The local loss of territorial security and dominance supports the warning setting, but not its Fire imagery.
Casting revelation behind their backs is a distant back image, unrelated to being unable to shield the back from Fire.
It warns that leaning toward wrongdoers brings contact with Fire and ends with no aid, reinforcing both punishment and helplessness.
Putting the covenant behind their backs is an unrelated metaphor and adds no judgment-scene detail.
The following response to even a breath of punishment, their cry of woe and admission of wrongdoing, completes the local warning sequence.
The wish to return when seeing punishment conveys the belated realization implicit in the focus ayah's conditional knowledge.
The immediately following scales establish the just judgment setting but add no specific detail to the Fire's exposure.
It warns dissenters of trial or painful punishment, a broad admonitory parallel without the focus scene's details.
The challenge to plot without respite offers a limited parallel of enemies unable to secure a delay.
It contrasts divine watchfulness with the disbelievers' misguidance, without clarifying their inability to fend off Fire.
The Hour arrives suddenly when later remembrance cannot benefit, closely matching the focus ayah's too-late knowledge.
Its conditional worldly punishment of disbelievers is only a broad punishment connection.
It explicitly assigns the Fire as their abode and denies them helpers, reinforcing the final lack of aid.
Its account of the Fire's guardians and its testing function is related but does not explain the threatened bodily exposure.
Remaining in the Fire without release extends the consequence, but repeats the helpless punitive outcome already established.
The prohibition on certain questions from believers does not illuminate the disbelievers' Fire scene.
The statement that the Book is sent down from God does not add to the warning.
God's power to restrain the disbelievers' violence supplies only a remote contrast to their own lack of defense.
The fixed staring eyes and empty hearts of terrified wrongdoers give a bodily image of helpless judgment exposure.
The hypocrites' excuses for not joining an expedition do not clarify the focus ayah.
The arrival of punishment in the warned people's courtyard parallels the promised punishment becoming inescapably present.
The command to turn away for a time offers no substantive detail about the threatened Fire.
Its restraint of worldly fighting is a distant contrary case of protection from violence.
The assurance that they will know the report after a time loosely echoes the focus ayah's conditional knowledge.
Their demand to hasten the punishment directly resembles the local demand for the promised warning.
The universal mission as bearer of warning supplies only the broad preaching frame.
The promise that they will see later is a limited counterpart to knowing the reality when it arrives.
The signs given to Jesus and restraint of his opponents do not explain the Fire's exposure of disbelievers.
This repeated promise that they will see later adds little beyond the prior parallel.
The sacred-month ruling and command concerning fighting are unrelated to this judgment scene.
The repeated command to turn away for a time adds no detail to the focus warning.
On seeing punishment, wrongdoers receive neither relief nor delay, reinforcing its irreversibility.
On the decisive Day the disbelievers' faith will not benefit and they receive no respite, clarifying the too-late realization.
Wealth and children cannot avail disbelievers, who become fuel for the Fire, supplying the wider helplessness of the condemned.
It similarly denies that wealth and children avail disbelievers and identifies their abiding in the Fire.
It states that punishment is not lightened and they are not helped, directly reinforcing the focus ayah's lack of aid.
The lowest depth of the Fire and absence of any helper intensify the stated abandonment.
The nonacceptance of repentance after increased disbelief concerns a related finality but not the Fire's immediate exposure.
Being dragged upon their faces in the Fire gives a close, concrete parallel to unprotected facial exposure.
The refusal of ransom and assignment to the Fire give another aspect of the disbelievers' inability to escape judgment.
Faces being turned over in the Fire closely specifies the focus ayah's facial vulnerability and adds their regretful speech.
It directly depicts faces thrown into the Fire as requital, a close parallel to the focus warning.
The disbelievers' hostile faces on hearing revelation and the promised Fire connect their present reaction to its threatened end.
Its bare statement that disbelievers deny is only a general description of those addressed in the focus ayah.
Their inability to leave the Fire adds a final consequence but is less specific than the earlier Fire parallels.
Fire cauterizing foreheads and backs closely parallels the focus ayah's exposed faces and backs.
It identifies disbelievers as lasting companions of the Fire but adds no detail about its inescapability.
Showing off in worship has no meaningful connection to the focus warning.
The military instruction involving vigilance behind the group is a worldly setting, not the eschatological Fire exposure.
The account of sorcery and its harmful teaching does not clarify the focus ayah.
It links disbelief and denial of resurrection with the Fire, but does not add to the exposure or lack of help.
Neglect of prayer does not materially clarify the focus ayah.
The statement that those who disbelieved will soon know offers only a terse echo of the focus ayah's realization.
The idolaters' mutual repudiation, Fire abode, and lack of helpers reinforce the failure of all support at judgment.
Repeated calamity near disbelievers' homes until God's promise arrives develops the certainty and approach of the warning.
The warning against being distracted by wealth and children addresses believers and does not clarify this scene.
A Fire enclosing wrongdoers and scorching faces gives a particularly close image of total, unshieldable exposure.
Its final mention of apostates as lasting companions of the Fire is too broad and contextually distant.
Misguided worldly effort does not add to the focus ayah's threatened punishment.
The statement of divine sovereignty and knowledge does not materially explain the disbelievers' Fire exposure.
The detailed nursing and family-maintenance ruling is unrelated to the focus ayah.
The summons to a terrible matter on the Day provides a broad judgment horizon only.
The Fire closed over them gives a concise parallel of comprehensive confinement and inescapability.
The exhortation against self-purification and notice of divine forgiveness does not clarify the warning.
Turning away retreating does not materially illuminate the focus ayah.
The dress and modesty directives are unrelated to the threatened Fire scene.
The prohibition on alliances with hostile disbelievers does not clarify their judgment exposure.
The charge of disbelief and associating partners gives only the general culpability behind the warning.
Its repeated burning of the disbelievers' skins specifies the Fire as an inescapable bodily punishment.
The Fire as both bed and covering gives a comprehensive image of the condemned being surrounded without protection.
Gathering the disbelievers upon their faces and feeding Hell whenever it subsides closely develops facial exposure and confinement.
The criminal's entry into Hell, where he neither dies nor lives, clarifies the enduring consequence of the warning.
Garments of Fire and boiling water poured over heads give a close physical parallel to the focus ayah's unshieldable bodily exposure.
The Fire's sight of them from afar and its raging sound intensify the imminence of the threatened encounter.
Being bound in a constricted place of Fire and calling for destruction gives a strong image of helpless punishment.
Those who try to leave the Fire are returned to it, making explicit the impossibility of repelling or escaping it.
The command to enter the Hell they used to deny directly matches the focus ayah's contrast between present denial and future knowledge.
Layers of Fire above and below them give a direct image of total enclosure with no side from which to find protection.
The blackened faces of those who lied against God provide a related facial sign of final judgment.
The chains and yokes on their necks portray the loss of all agency that accompanies the focus ayah's lack of help.
Their being dragged through boiling water and then burned in the Fire gives a direct punitive sequel to the threatened exposure.
The guilty remaining in Hell without relief develops the permanence of the punishment.
Their violent thrusting into the Fire supplies a direct transition from warning to forced entry into it.
Sinners recognized by their marks and seized by forelocks and feet gives a bodily judgment image related to exposed faces and backs.
The hospitality of the denier in a burning Fire directly identifies the outcome of denial.
Its description of the fierce angels guarding the Fire reinforces that the condemned will find no rescuing aid there.
The promised punishment of Hell for those who disbelieve supplies the general destination stated conditionally in the focus ayah.
The blazing Fire stripping away the scalp gives a particularly close image of a person unable to preserve the head from it.
The declaration of entry into Saqar offers a concise, direct counterpart to the focus ayah's Fire warning.
Hell lying in wait for transgressors frames it as the prepared destination of those who reject the warning.
Entering a scorching Fire is a terse direct parallel to the Fire the disbelievers will be unable to ward off.
The intensely hot Fire gives a compact direct characterization of the threatened punishment.
God's kindled Fire, which rises over hearts, adds an image of punishment penetrating the condemned rather than remaining wardable outside them.
The promise that the denier will enter a flaming Fire gives a concise parallel judgment outcome.
